content: Urticaria, commonly known as hives, is a condition characterized by the appearance of raised, red, itchy welts on the skin. These welts can vary in size and may appear anywhere on the body. The condition is classified into two main types: spontaneous urticaria and physical urticaria. Spontaneous urticaria is further divided into acute and chronic forms based on the duration of symptoms. Acute urticaria typically lasts for a few hours to several weeks, while chronic urticaria persists for six weeks or longer. Physical urticaria, on the other hand, is triggered by external factors such as mechanical pressure, temperature changes, or other physical stimuli. Subtypes of physical urticaria include dermographic urticaria, delayed pressure urticaria, cold contact urticaria, heat contact urticaria, solar urticaria, and vibratory urticaria. Additionally, there are other specific types of urticaria, such as cholinergic urticaria, adrenergic urticaria, aquagenic urticaria, contact urticaria, and drug-induced urticaria. The pathophysiology of urticaria involves complex mechanisms, many of which are still under investigation. Inflammatory processes driven by increased immune cell activity play a significant role. Key immune cells implicated in urticaria include basophils, mast cells, macrophages, neutrophils, and T cells. Among these, basophils and mast cells are particularly important, as their activation is often linked to intracellular signaling defects or autoimmune disorders. Immunoglobulin E (IgE) autoantibodies, such as IgE anti-IL-24, have been identified in patients with chronic spontaneous urticaria. The complement system also contributes to the pathogenesis of chronic spontaneous urticaria, with components like C3, C4, and C5 playing established roles. Genetic factors may also influence urticaria, as studies have reported upregulation of 506 genes and downregulation of 51 genes in affected skin. Many of these genes are involved in adhesion (e.g., SELE), cell activation (e.g., CD69), and chemotaxis (e.g., CCL2). Urticaria is also associated with autoimmune diseases such as Hashimoto's thyroiditis, mastocytosis (e.g., urticaria pigmentosa), atopic conditions (e.g., atopic dermatitis, hay fever, allergic asthma), systemic lupus erythematosus, and angioedema. The causes of urticaria can be idiopathic or related to immunological disorders, including autoimmune diseases, food allergies, medications, and infections. Non-immunological triggers, such as physical stimuli, dietary pseudo-allergens, and hereditary factors, can also contribute to its development. Differentiating urticaria from other conditions is crucial for effective treatment. Differential diagnoses include hereditary or acquired C1 complement deficiency, cutaneous mastocytosis (e.g., urticaria pigmentosa), malignancies, connective tissue diseases, angioedema, and exercise-induced anaphylaxis. Epidemiologically, urticaria affects individuals of all age groups, but it is most common in those aged 20–40 years. Females are more frequently affected than males, with an overall female-to-male ratio of approximately 2:1. However, delayed pressure urticaria is an exception, as it is more common in males, with a male-to-female ratio of 2:1. There is no racial predilection for urticaria. Risk factors for developing urticaria include atopy, air pollution, female gender, certain foods, medications, and specific occupations. The natural history, complications, and prognosis of urticaria depend on factors such as age, gender, urticaria subtype, and the presence of concurrent angioedema. Remission rates range from 10% to 60% within the first 5–10 years of diagnosis. Treatments generally alleviate symptoms in most cases, and the mean duration of urticaria varies among subtypes. Complications may include superimposed bacterial infections, anaphylaxis, and excoriation due to intense itching. Prognosis is generally better in patients younger than 19 years, while factors such as female gender, prolonged disease duration at initial presentation, concurrent angioedema, physical urticaria, cholinergic urticaria, and chronic NSAID use are associated with worse outcomes. Diagnosis of urticaria involves a thorough history and physical examination. Acute urticaria typically appears minutes after allergen exposure and lasts from a few hours to several weeks, while chronic urticaria persists for at least six weeks. Symptoms include the spontaneous appearance of wheals, often triggered by food, allergens, exercise, medications, or skin pressure, depending on the subtype. Common symptoms include wheals and pruritus, while less common symptoms include dizziness, nausea, headache, and burning sensations. Physical examination reveals raised, red, itchy welts approximately 5 mm in diameter, which can appear anywhere on the body. Laboratory evaluations can help assess disease severity, treatment response, and prognosis. Tests such as the autologous serum skin test (ASST) and basophil activation test (BAT) are useful for detecting autoantibodies against IgE. Elevated levels of C-reactive protein (CRP), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), certain interleukins, and tumor necrosis factor-alpha have been reported in urticaria patients. Diagnostic tools like the urticaria activity score (UAS7) questionnaire assess the severity of spontaneous urticaria, while the ice cube test is used to diagnose cold-induced urticaria by observing wheal formation after cold exposure. Treatment of urticaria typically begins with H1 antihistamines, such as diphenhydramine, hydroxyzine, cetirizine, and other similar medications. Some patients may require higher doses of antihistamines for complete symptom control, which are generally well-tolerated. If first-line antihistamines fail, second-line treatments like omalizumab and cyclosporine are recommended. Omalizumab has shown efficacy in various urticaria subtypes, including solar urticaria, cold urticaria, cholinergic urticaria, urticarial vasculitis, and symptomatic dermographic urticaria. Alternative treatments include dapsone, hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine, colchicine, methotrexate, intravenous gamma globulin, plasmapheresis, corticosteroids, H2 antagonists, and leukotriene antagonists. Specific alternative treatments may be recommended for different urticaria subtypes. Primary prevention involves identifying and avoiding specific triggers that lead to wheal development, such as food allergens, cold temperatures, or sharp edges. This approach can reduce the severity and frequency of urticaria attacks.
